summary: Experimental document on synchronizing service boundaries and mapping elements between servers using the Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) protocol. LoST maps a location to a service, such as the right emergency call center. This keeps the servers' data consistent.

plainLanguage.summary: When someone calls an emergency number, the call has to go to the right answer centre for the place the caller is. Each provider's server knows the area it covers. This RFC defines a small XML protocol so that those servers can tell each other when their maps change, either by asking for what is missing or by pushing an update. It works whether or not the LoST protocol itself is used for the lookup.

questions: how to sync lost mapping data
how do lost servers synchronize mappings
subtitle: An XML protocol for keeping the service boundaries of emergency services in step between LoST servers.

tldr.problem: Each emergency services server holds a map of the area it covers and the answering point that serves it. When several providers run such servers in different places, their maps drift apart and a call could be routed to the wrong place.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reuses the mapping element defined for LoST and defines an XML protocol with two exchanges between a LoST Sync source and a LoST Sync destination: a pull request for the mappings the destination is missing, and a push of new or deleted mappings.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document that registers a media type and an XML namespace for the protocol. It has since been updated by RFC 8996, which deprecates TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1.

facts.label: Transport
facts.value: HTTPS with the POST method, with no fallback to HTTP

facts.label: How a mapping is identified
facts.value: The source, sourceId and lastUpdated attributes

today: RFC 6739 was published in October 2012 as an Experimental document. It has since been updated by RFC 8996, which deprecates TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1.

sections.title: What LoST Sync Is For
sections.content:
Since the early days of emergency services there has been a desire to route emergency calls to the Public Safety Answering Points nearest to the location of the caller. For this purpose each answer point discloses one or more service boundaries, so that the information can be used to select the right answer point and route the call to it. RFC 5222 defines a service boundary as the region within which all locations map to the same service URI or set of URIs for a given service, and it may consist of several non-contiguous geometric shapes. RFC 5222 also specifies the data structure itself, the mapping element.

This document reuses that existing data structure and defines an XML-based protocol to exchange authoritative service boundaries between two entities, the LoST Sync source and the LoST Sync destination. The protocol can be used whether or not the LoST protocol itself is used for querying service boundary information.

The RFC also sets out its own terminology. It reuses terms introduced by the mapping architecture document, such as coverage region, forest guide, mapping and authoritative mapping server, and it uses the term ESRP for an Emergency Services Routing Proxy. The exchange always runs between a LoST Sync source and a LoST Sync destination: in the examples, Node A holds the mappings that Node B is going to retrieve, so Node A is the source for the data and Node B the destination.
sections.plainLanguage: Each emergency services server holds a set of mapping records. A mapping says which area a server covers and which service URI belongs to that area. This RFC is about getting those records from one server to another so the two do not disagree about where an emergency call should go.

sections.title: How LoST Servers Are Arranged
sections.content:
The RFC's worked example places LoST in two countries, Austria and Finland. Austria runs three authoritative mapping servers, labelled East, West and Vienna, where the first two cover the whole country except Vienna, which is covered by a separate LoST server. Finland deploys a single LoST server that also acts as a forest guide. Only one service is assumed, urn:service:sos, since otherwise the number of stored mappings would have to be multiplied by the number of services in use.

In the LoST mapping architecture, LoST servers cooperate to provide an ubiquitous, globally scalable and resilient mapping service, and they can peer, meaning they have an ongoing data exchange relationship. Peering relationships are set up manually, based on local policies, and a LoST server may peer with any number of others. Forest guides peer with other forest guides; authoritative mapping servers peer with forest guides and with other authoritative servers, either in the same cluster or above or below them in the tree. Authoritative mapping servers push coverage regions up the tree, from child nodes to parent nodes, so the child tells the parent which geospatial or civic region it covers for a given service.

The LoST Sync mechanism can run between the two forest guides. The three mappings stored in the Austrian forest guide are then sent to the Finnish one, and the single mapping in the Finnish forest guide is sent to the Austrian one. The three Austrian LoST servers could also use LoST Sync to tell the Austrian forest guide about their boundaries. Those authoritative mapping servers remain responsible for maintaining their own mapping information. Because the amount of data exchanged is small and the expected rate of change is low, the nodes are configured to exchange all their mapping information whenever a change happens.
sections.plainLanguage: LoST servers are arranged in a tree. The servers that know the detail about an area sit at the bottom, and forest guides sit above them holding a summarised view. The RFC's example has three servers under an Austrian forest guide and one Finnish server that is also its own forest guide. The two guides can use this protocol to keep each other's summaries in step.

sections.title: Querying for Mappings
sections.content:
A LoST Sync destination has two ways to retrieve mapping elements from a LoST Sync source. When the destination has no mappings at all, it submits an empty getMappingsRequest, which asks for all mappings from the source. That request does not propagate further to other nodes. When the destination already holds mappings from previous exchanges, it may instead send a getMappingsRequest with one or more exists child elements, each holding a mapping fingerprint with the source, sourceId and lastUpdated attributes of a mapping the destination already has. The source then returns only the mappings that are missing at the destination or have been updated. When to poll is left to local policy and is outside the scope of the document.

After issuing the request, the destination waits for the getMappingsResponse. On a successful response it stores the received mappings and works out which ones to update. On the source side, an empty request means all locally available mappings MUST be returned. A request with exists elements means the source MUST consult its local mapping database to determine whether any of the client's mappings are stale and whether there are mappings it does not yet have. Staleness is found by looking for mappings with the same source and sourceId attributes where a mapping with a more recent lastUpdated date exists.

Processing a request may lead to a successful response or to an errors message. Only the badRequest, forbidden, internalError and serverTimeout errors defined in RFC 5222 are used. Neither the redirect nor the warnings messages are reused.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to ask. A server that has nothing asks for everything. A server that already has some records sends the fingerprints of the ones it holds, and the other side replies only with what is new or what has changed since.

sections.title: Pushing Mappings to a Peer
sections.content:
When a LoST Sync source obtains new information of interest to its peers, it may push the new mappings to them. Configuration at both peers decides whether this is used and what is pushed to whom. New mappings may arrive through a manual addition to the local database or through interaction with other entities, and deleting a mapping may also trigger an exchange.

The source SHOULD keep track of which destinations it has pushed mappings to. If it keeps no state, it always has to push the complete data set. Mapping elements are identified by the source, sourceID and lastUpdated attributes, and a mapping is considered the same if these three match. A pushMappings request MUST contain one or more mapping elements.

To delete a mapping, the content of the mapping is left empty, so that the mapping element contains only the source, sourceID, lastUpdated and expires attributes. The expires attribute is required by the schema but is ignored when the receiver processes the request. On receiving a push, the destination inspects its cache to decide whether the mapping updates an existing one, creates a new one, or should be discarded. A newly received mapping with a more recent lastUpdated attribute MUST update an existing mapping with matching source and sourceID attributes. A mapping that matches nothing on source and sourceId MUST be added to the local cache as an independent mapping. If a request to delete arrives and no mapping can be identified, an errors response MUST be returned containing the notDeleted child element, which MAY carry a message attribute for debugging and MUST contain the mapping elements that caused the error. A successful push is answered with a pushMappingsResponse that returns no additional elements.

The RFC also warns about loops when more than two servers use the mechanism, and explains how they are avoided. Implementations MUST NOT modify mappings they receive, so a mapping that has travelled through a third server is recognised as already held and the update can be ignored. It also notes that if the set of synchronising nodes does not form a tree, the same information can arrive through several other nodes, which is unavoidable but generally only imposes a modest overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: When a record changes, the server that knows about the change can send it straight to its peers. A deletion is sent as an empty record carrying only the identifiers of what to remove, and the receiving server reports back if it cannot find it. Records that pass through a third server are left exactly as received, so each server can tell that it has already seen them and will not pass them round again.

sections.title: Transport, Schema and Registrations
sections.content:
LoST Sync needs a transport to carry requests and responses. This document uses HTTPS to exchange XML documents, and provides no fallback to HTTP. When HTTP is run over TLS, LoST Sync messages use the POST method, and requests MUST use the Cache-Control response directive no-cache. All LoST Sync responses, including those indicating a warning or an error, are carried in 2xx responses, typically 200. The 3xx, 4xx and 5xx HTTP response codes indicate that the request itself failed or was redirected, and those responses do not contain any LoST Sync XML elements.

The message format is defined as a RELAX NG schema. To avoid copying pattern definitions from the LoST schema, that schema is included as lost.rng. The grammar accepts a choice of four top-level elements: pushMappings, pushMappingsResponse, getMappingsRequest and getMappingsResponse. A pushMappings element holds one or more mapping elements; a pushMappingsResponse holds only an extension point; a getMappingsRequest holds either one or more exists elements, each containing one or more mapping-fingerprint elements with source, sourceId and lastUpdated attributes, or an extension point; and a getMappingsResponse holds one or more mapping elements.

IANA has registered the media type application/lostsync+xml, with no required parameters, an optional charset parameter as in application/xml, and a file extension of .lostsyncxml. The RELAX NG schema is registered under the URI urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:lostsync1, and the namespace under urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:lostsync1.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages travel over an encrypted HTTPS connection, using the POST method and never cached. The document also fixes the shape of the XML, so that a sender and a receiver can agree on what a request, a response or an error looks like, and it registers the file type and the XML names used.

sections.title: Signed Mappings and Threats
sections.content:
The protocol exchanges authoritative mapping information between two entities, so the operations described require authentication of neighbouring nodes. The LoST Sync clients and servers MUST implement TLS and use it. The RFC notes that TLS version 1.2 is the most recent version at the time of writing but has very limited actual deployment and might not be readily available in tool kits, while TLS version 1.0 is the most widely deployed version and will give the broadest interoperability. Mutual authentication between source and destination is not necessarily required in all deployments, unless an emergency service authority wants to enforce access control before the distribution of their mapping elements, which may be the case when certain emergency services networks distribute internal mappings that are not meant for public distribution.

Because mappings carry authority, they must be signed. To avoid the possibility of an untrustworthy member claiming a coverage region for which it is not authorized, authoritative mapping servers MUST sign the mappings they distribute using an XML digital signature, and a recipient MUST verify that the signing entity is indeed authorized to speak for that region. In many cases this requires an out-of-band agreement about which entities take on that role. Determining who can speak for a region is inherently difficult unless there is a small set of authorizing entities that participants can trust. Receiving systems should be particularly suspicious if an existing coverage region is replaced by a new one containing a different value in the uri element, and because mappings are signed they cannot be modified by intermediate LoST servers.

The RFC also describes what a compromised or misconfigured server can do. A denial of service can follow an injected mapping. If the mapping data contains a URL that does not exist, then emergency services for the indicated area are not reachable. If all the mapping data points to a single answer point rather than a large number of them, that answer point is likely to experience overload. And if the mapping data points to a server controlled by an adversary, it might impersonate answer points. For unusual changes to the mapping database, approval by a system administrator of the emergency services infrastructure, or a similar expert, may be required before any mappings are installed.
sections.plainLanguage: The two servers must authenticate each other over TLS, and the mapping records themselves must be signed, so that a server cannot claim to cover an area it is not entitled to cover. The danger the RFC warns about is a server that injects a record pointing emergency calls at the wrong place, or at a single overloaded centre, or at a server the attacker controls.

messages.label: getMappingsRequest
messages.note: Empty to ask for everything, or carrying exists elements with mapping fingerprints to ask only for what is missing or changed.

messages.label: getMappingsResponse
messages.note: Returns the mappings, or an errors message with badRequest, forbidden, internalError or serverTimeout.

messages.label: pushMappings
messages.note: One or more mapping elements. An empty mapping element with only the identifying attributes requests a deletion.

messages.label: pushMappingsResponse
messages.note: An empty success response, or an errors message with a notDeleted element when a deletion could not be carried out.
